newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First voters back centre-left coalition - poll.
newsitem.headline: NZ First voters back centre-left coalition - poll.

text.p: New Zealand First voters remain strongly in favour of a deal with the centre-left Labour Party over the conservative National Party, according to a poll released on Friday.
Respondents in general preferred a Labour-led government, although they expected NZ First to go with National, the poll showed.

Nationalist New Zealand First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is negotiating separately with both Labour and National over the shape of the next government. It has not declared a preference for a deal with either.

The UMR-Insight poll, published in the National Business Review, showed 55 percent of NZ First voters would prefer a deal with Labour supported by the left wing Alliance, while 23 percent favoured a coalition with National backed by free-market advocates Act New Zealand.
In a similar poll taken shortly after the election, 62 percent of NZ First voters backed an arrangement with Labour against 22 percent preferring a deal with National.

National has 44 MPs, Labour 37, NZ First 17, the Alliance 13 and Act eight. National and NZ First, which together would have 61 seats in the 120 seat parliament, are the only two parties which could form a majority government without the support of others.

The poll showed that among the combined supporters of all parties, 43 percent favoured a Labour-led government (down from 45 percent in October) and 38 percent wanted National to lead the governing coalition (up from 37 percent).
But when respondents were asked who they expected NZ First to choose, 45 percent said National against 22 percent who said Labour, with 29 percent unsure.
Negotiations over the shape of the next government have now ended their fifth week.

The poll, taken last weekend after four weeks of talks, showed 62 percent thought it was time for NZ First to decide which party it would support in government. Thirty percent said it was reasonable to take time, maybe until Christmas, to settle matters.
The poll sampled 750 respondents and had a margin of error of 3.5 percent.
